opus-5.5.text:
I think the original aspiration was actually quite simple: I wanted machine learning to be something that more people could really use. When I started out as a student, I was excited by the models themselves, the algorithms, the math. But I kept running into the same wall. A great idea on paper doesn't matter much if it takes weeks to run, or only works on one particular machine, or requires a huge engineering team to deploy.

So gradually my focus shifted toward the systems side: how do we build tools that make these methods fast, scalable, and accessible? That's what drove projects like XGBoost early on. It wasn't about inventing a fundamentally new learning theory; it was about taking a good method and engineering it so that people could apply it to real problems at scale. Seeing data scientists everywhere pick it up and win competitions or ship products with it was incredibly rewarding.

Later, the same motivation led to work on deep learning frameworks and compilers like TVM. Hardware was diversifying very quickly, with GPUs, mobile chips, and specialized accelerators, and models were changing just as fast. I felt there had to be a more automatic and principled way to bridge that gap, instead of hand-tuning everything for each new combination.

If I had to summarize it, the aspiration is democratization. I'd like AI to run well anywhere, on any device, for anyone, not just inside a few large data centers. And I've always believed open source is a big part of that, because the best systems are built by a community, not by one person or one company.

r001.rationale: The response describes making machine learning accessible and AI usable by anyone, but does not identify the aspiration as enabling people to create the AI systems they themselves want.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I think the original aspiration was really about accessibility, about closing the gap between what the algorithms could do and what people could actually run.

When I was a student, I kept noticing that the bottleneck in machine learning was rarely the idea. The idea was often on a whiteboard already. The hard part was getting it to run efficiently, on the hardware you actually had, at the scale you actually needed. If you wanted gradient boosting on a big dataset, or deep learning on something other than one specific vendor's GPU, you hit a wall that had nothing to do with research and everything to do with systems.

So with XGBoost, the question was simple: can we make a very good algorithm fast enough and robust enough that a single person on a laptop can use it, and a company can use the same code at scale? Then with MXNet and later TVM, it became a bigger version of the same question. There are many kinds of hardware, many frameworks, many models. Can we build the compiler layer that lets any model run well on any device, without a team of engineers hand-tuning every kernel?

Underneath all of it is one belief. Machine learning should not be a privilege of people with the biggest clusters. If you democratize the systems layer, you democratize who gets to participate. That's still what drives me today, especially with large language models, where the pressure to centralize is stronger than ever. I want to make sure the open, run-it-anywhere path stays viable.

r001.rationale: The candidate describes making machine learning more accessible and enabling people to run models across hardware, but does not say the aspiration was to let everyone create the AI systems they themselves want.

astra-6.text: The original aspiration was to make machine learning more accessible. If you have an idea, you should be able to try it without having to build all the infrastructure yourself or understand every detail of the hardware underneath. That’s what drew me to AI systems: building tools that help people turn their ideas into something that actually runs. And through open source, those tools can become something a whole community builds on and improves together.

r001.rationale: The response says the aspiration was to make machine learning accessible so people could try their ideas without building infrastructure and turn them into something that runs, conveying the ability to create the AI systems they want.

sol-6.1.text: The original aspiration was to make machine learning more accessible. A good idea shouldn’t require a huge engineering team or specialized infrastructure before someone can try it. I was interested in building systems that close that gap—so researchers and developers can take an idea, experiment with it, and turn it into something useful. That means making the tools efficient, but also making them open and easy for others to build on.

r001.rationale: The response says the goal was to make machine learning more accessible so researchers and developers could experiment with ideas and build useful things. It does not clearly state the specific aspiration of enabling everyone to create the AI systems they themselves want.
